title: Buchberger criterion from strict standard representations
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $r\geq1$, and $S=k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. Let $\prec$ be a total well-order on $\mathbf N^r$, with $0$ least, preserved by addition. For $0\ne f\in S$, let $\operatorname{LM}(f)$ be its greatest support exponent and $\operatorname{LC}(f)$ its coefficient there. Let $B\subset S$ be any set of nonzero monic polynomials, where monic means $\operatorname{LC}(b)=1$; $B$ need not be finite or homogeneous. For $b,c\in B$, put $\lambda(b,c)_a=\max(\operatorname{LM}(b)_a,\operatorname{LM}(c)_a)$ and $P(b,c)=x^{\lambda(b,c)-\operatorname{LM}(b)}b-x^{\lambda(b,c)-\operatorname{LM}(c)}c$. Suppose that for every $b,c\in B$ there are polynomials $q_u$ indexed by $u\in B$, only finitely many nonzero, such that $P(b,c)=\sum_{u\in B}q_u u$ and $\operatorname{LM}(q_u u)\prec\lambda(b,c)$ whenever $q_u u\ne0$. Then every nonzero $f$ in the ideal $(B)$ generated by $B$ has some $b\in B$ with $\operatorname{LM}(b)_a\leq\operatorname{LM}(f)_a$ for every coordinate $a$. The empty set $B$ is allowed.

source.place: Lecture 7, Theorem 4.11 and its proof using Lemma 4.12; arbitrary-family, strict-standard-representation form supplied by the agent (each polynomial representation has finite support). Local document WANTED; primary lecture notes read online; no Stacks tag asserted.

proof.text:
The finite sums $\sum_i q_i b_i$, with $q_i\in S$ and $b_i\in B$, form an ideal: sums concatenate the lists, negatives negate the coefficients, and multiplication by $s\in S$ replaces $q_i$ by $sq_i$. They contain $B$ and lie in every ideal containing $B$, so they are exactly $(B)$. Expanding each $q_i$ coefficientwise gives a finite representation $f=\sum_{i\in I}c_i x^{\alpha_i}b_i$, with $c_i\in k\setminus\{0\}$; repeated $b_i$ are permitted. If $B=\varnothing$, the ideal is zero and the conclusion is vacuous. Otherwise fix $0
e f\in(B)$; every such representation has a nonempty finite $I$.

source.place: Lecture 7, Theorem 4.11 converse and Lemma 4.12; agent finite-support adaptation to arbitrary B, read online at https://lekili.duckdns.org/teaching/calg/lec07.html; local copy WANTED.

proof.text: For any representation from step 1 put $\delta_i=\alpha_i+\operatorname{LM}(b_i)$ and $\delta=\max_{i\in I}\delta_i$ in the monomial order. Translating the support of $b_i$ by $\alpha_i$ preserves its strict order, so $c_i x^{\alpha_i}b_i$ has leading exponent $\delta_i$ and coefficient $c_i$, since $b_i$ is monic. Every exponent in $f$ is at most $\delta$: coefficientwise addition cannot introduce an exponent absent from every summand. Among all finite representations choose one whose $\delta$ is least; it exists because the set of their maxima is nonempty and $\prec$ is a well-order. Write $T=\{i\in I:\delta_i=\delta\}$, which is nonempty.

source.place: Lecture 7, Theorem 4.11 converse and Lemma 4.12; agent finite-support adaptation to arbitrary B, read online at https://lekili.duckdns.org/teaching/calg/lec07.html; local copy WANTED.

proof.text:
If $\operatorname{LM}(f)=\delta$, choose $i\in T$. Then $\operatorname{LM}(f)=\alpha_i+\operatorname{LM}(b_i)$, so $b_i$ gives the required coordinatewise divisibility. To rule out the remaining case, suppose $\operatorname{LM}(f)\prec\delta$. The coefficient of $x^\delta$ in $f$ is zero. Terms with $i
otin T$ have no such coefficient, and each term with $i\in T$ has that coefficient $c_i$. Hence $\sum_{i\in T}c_i=0$. Put $H=\sum_{i\in T}c_i x^{\alpha_i}b_i$ and fix $j\in T$.

source.place: Lecture 7, Theorem 4.11 converse and Lemma 4.12; agent finite-support adaptation to arbitrary B, read online at https://lekili.duckdns.org/teaching/calg/lec07.html; local copy WANTED.

proof.text:
For $i\in T\setminus\{j\}$ let $\lambda_i=\operatorname{LM}(b_i)\vee\operatorname{LM}(b_j)$, the coordinatewise maximum. Since $\alpha_i+\operatorname{LM}(b_i)=\alpha_j+\operatorname{LM}(b_j)=\delta$, both leading exponents are coordinatewise at most $\delta$; thus $\lambda_i\leq\delta$ coordinatewise. Expanding the definition of $P$ gives $x^{\delta-\lambda_i}P(b_i,b_j)=x^{\alpha_i}b_i-x^{\alpha_j}b_j$. Therefore, by $\sum_{i\in T}c_i=0$,
$$H=\sum_{i\in T\setminus\{j\}}c_i x^{\delta-\lambda_i}P(b_i,b_j).$$
Indeed the coefficient of $x^{\alpha_j}b_j$ on the right is $-\sum_{i
e j}c_i=c_j$. This is a distributive identity, also valid if some $b_i=b_j$; no independent cancellation theorem is invoked.

source.place: Lecture 7, Theorem 4.11 converse and Lemma 4.12; agent finite-support adaptation to arbitrary B, read online at https://lekili.duckdns.org/teaching/calg/lec07.html; local copy WANTED.

proof.text:
For each of the finitely many pairs in step 4 use the hypothesis to choose $P(b_i,b_j)=\sum_{u\in B}q_{iu}u$, with finite support and $\operatorname{LM}(q_{iu}u)\prec\lambda_i$ whenever $q_{iu}u
e0$. By [lem-sfb-monomial-order-leading-product], nonzero factors have the sum of their leading exponents. Its leading-coefficient formula also shows that a product of nonzero polynomials is nonzero: the two leading coefficients are nonzero in the field. Consequently, if $q_{iu}
e0$ and $\beta$ occurs in its support, then
$$\beta+\operatorname{LM}(u)\preceq\operatorname{LM}(q_{iu})+\operatorname{LM}(u)=\operatorname{LM}(q_{iu}u)\prec\lambda_i.$$
Adding $\delta-\lambda_i$ preserves the strict inequality and gives
$$\delta-\lambda_i+\beta+\operatorname{LM}(u)\prec\delta.$$
Here $(\delta-\lambda_i)+\lambda_i=\delta$ coordinatewise; this is why the coordinatewise bound in step 4 was checked.

source.place: Lecture 7, Theorem 4.11 converse and Lemma 4.12; agent finite-support adaptation to arbitrary B, read online at https://lekili.duckdns.org/teaching/calg/lec07.html; local copy WANTED.

proof.text:
In the fixed representation of $f$, replace the part $H$ by the right side of step 4 and substitute step 5. Expand every $q_{iu}$ into its finitely many monomials. Each resulting nonzero scalar-monomial multiple of $u\in B$ has leading exponent strictly below $\delta$ by the last inequality of step 5. Every unchanged term $i
otin T$ also has leading exponent strictly below $\delta$ by definition of $T$. There are finitely many terms: $T$ is finite, every chosen pair representation is finitely supported, and every coefficient polynomial has finite support. Delete zero scalar terms. The list is nonempty because its sum is $f
e0$; its finite maximum is strictly below $\delta$, contradicting minimality in step 2. Thus the case excluded in step 3 cannot occur, and the divisibility established there proves the assertion. The argument uses no finiteness or homogeneity assumption on $B$.

lean.statement: theorem buchberger_standard_representation_criterion {k : Type u} [Field k] {r : ℕ} (hr : 1 ≤ r) (m : MonomialOrder (Fin r)) (B : Set (MvPolynomial (Fin r) k)) (hB : ∀ b ∈ B, b ≠ 0 ∧ m.Monic b) (hS : ∀ b ∈ B, ∀ c ∈ B, ∃ q : B →₀ MvPolynomial (Fin r) k, m.sPolynomial b c = q.sum (fun u a ↦ a * (u : MvPolynomial (Fin r) k)) ∧ ∀ u : B, q u * (u : MvPolynomial (Fin r) k) ≠ 0 → m.toSyn (m.degree (q u * (u : MvPolynomial (Fin r) k))) < m.toSyn (m.degree b ⊔ m.degree c)) (f : MvPolynomial (Fin r) k) (hf : f ∈ Ideal.span B) (hf0 : f ≠ 0) : ∃ b ∈ B, ∀ a : Fin r, m.degree b a ≤ m.degree f a
